srcVerified.summary: _execute_parallelization's _proceed_branch and _cancel_branch have no except SubAgentChildPausedError handler, unlike the structurally-parallel _execute_orchestrator_workers, so a PARALLELIZATION branch's nested sub-agent pause is silently misclassified as an ordinary failure and its resumable state is discarded.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: A PARALLELIZATION workflow has a SUB_AGENT_DISPATCH branch whose child sub-workflow runs under cascade_policy=pause and hits a HITL gate (or effect-fence-ambiguous pause) mid-flight, raising SubAgentChildPausedError (workflow_driver_types.py:156). In _proceed_branch (line 7787 `except Exception:`) or _cancel_branch (line 8011 `except Exception as _exc:`), this exception has no dedicated branch (compare _execute_orchestrator_workers' _proceed_worker/_cancel_worker at lines 10908 and 11171, which explicitly do `except SubAgentChildPausedError as _paused: paused_child_dispositions[branch_index] = _paused.child_snapshot`). The branch is instead recorded as an ordinary 'completed'/no-output terminal, and `_paused.child_snapshot` (the child's resumable cursor including any pending HITL request) is never read or stored anywhere, so it is permanently lost. Additionally, PeerFanOutResumeState (pause_resume_protocol_types.py:304-351), the PARALLELIZATION resume-snapshot carrier, has no `paused_child_branches` field at all (unlike FanOutResumeState line 256), so even if caught there would be no place to persist it. On any resume of the parent run, this branch is permanently treated as a terminal failure with no output; the child sub-workflow (and any pending human-approval request inside it) can never be resumed, silently stranding its already-completed work.

This defeats the entire purpose of the F5 signing-key/audit-signature mechanism (non-repudiation/tamper-evidence for the highest compliance tier) — a forged or corrupted audit entry is indistinguishable from a genuine one at read-time verification.

srcVerified.summary: construct_sibling_ledger_entry builds action_id via unseparated string concatenation, creating a collision risk between distinct (parent_action_id, sibling_thread_id, step_index) triples, unlike the properly \x1f-delimited idempotency_key computed two lines below.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: action_id = f"{parent_action_id}{sibling_thread_id}{step_index}" with no delimiter. For example parent_action_id="run1", sibling_thread_id="0", step_index=23 yields "run1023"; parent_action_id="run10", sibling_thread_id="2", step_index=3 also yields "run1023" — two logically distinct sibling ledger entries collide on action_id, which anchors the F2 hash-chained ledger identity. Any downstream code that keys on action_id (dedup, replay lookup, audit trail linkage) would conflate the two entries. The idempotency_key computed immediately below via `_sibling_idempotency_key` correctly uses an \x1f-joined tuple specifically to avoid this class of ambiguity, indicating the action_id construction is an oversight rather than intentional.

verdict.rationale:
Confirmed as a real defect. Read harness-cp/src/harness_cp/sibling_ledger_entry_composition.py:149 directly: `action_id = f"{parent_action_id}{sibling_thread_id}{step_index}"` is indeed unseparated concatenation, while `_sibling_idempotency_key` two lines below (lines 150-152) correctly uses `"\x1f".join(...)`. The failure scenario's arithmetic checks out: parent_action_id='run1'+sibling_thread_id='0'+step_index=23 -> 'run1023', and parent_action_id='run10'+sibling_thread_id='2'+step_index=3 -> 'run1023' — genuine collision.

This is not a misreading or intentional/harmless behavior:
1. IS spec (design-substrate/Spec_Information_Substrate_v1.md line 392, C-IS-05 §5) formally declares action_id must be "Unique within the ledger" — a hard invariant, not aspirational prose.
2. Elsewhere in this exact codebase (harness-cp/src/harness_cp/workflow_driver_types.py, `compose_branch_step_action_id`), engineers explicitly guard against this identical collision class using delimited composition (`f"{parent_context.parent_action_id}:branch:{branch_index}:step:{local_step_index}"`), with an inline comment stating verbatim: "a step inside a branch must NOT reuse the flat action_id shape — N sibling branches at the same declared step_index would collide, breaking the IS §5 global-action_id-uniqueness invariant." This proves the collision class is a recognized, real risk this codebase otherwise takes care to avoid.
3. `Identifier` (harness-is/src/harness_is/state_ledger_entry_schema.py:32) is `NewType("Identifier", str)` — zero runtime uniqueness validation, so nothing catches a collision.
4. `construct_sibling_ledger_entry` is production-wired: harness-runtime/src/harness_runtime/lifecycle/cp_is_wiring.py `RuntimeCpIsWiring.emit_sibling_ledger_entry` calls it directly per the §12.3 seam.

One caveat worth noting for context: the actual write-path dedup in harness-is/src/harness_is/state_ledger_write.py `append_ledger_entry` keys exclusively on `idempotency_key` (properly delimited, collision-safe), not `action_id` — so the collision does NOT cause accidental IDEMPOTENT_NOOP or corrupt the hash chain at write time. But this does not refute the finding: action_id uniqueness is an independently-declared IS-spec invariant relied upon elsewhere (branch-causality resolution via parent_action_id lookups, audit trail linkage) exactly as the finding's failure_scenario describes, and the raw concatenation at line 149 can produce a real violation of that invariant. The finding's severity/category (high/correctness) and its inference that this is an oversight (given the properly-delimited idempotency_key two lines below) are well-supported.

srcVerified.failure_scenario: A live Managed Agents session runs to normal completion; Anthropic's API returns status="completed" (matching ManagedAgentSessionStatus.COMPLETED's own enum value "completed"). _status_from_anthropic's lookup dict only contains keys "idle", "running", "rescheduling", "terminated" (line 124-129), so "completed" falls through to the .get(..., ManagedAgentSessionStatus.FAILED) default and the session is reported as ManagedAgentSessionStatus.FAILED. Downstream, managed_agents_dispatch.py's _SUCCESS_STATUSES = {IDLE, COMPLETED} vs the full _TERMINAL_STATUSES set treats FAILED as a non-success terminal outcome, so the dispatcher raises RT-FAIL-MANAGED-AGENTS-SESSION / fails the workflow step for a vendor session that actually succeeded and was billed. srcVerified.summary: SyncDispatcherFacade.dispatch() does not cancel the coroutine it scheduled onto the outer event loop when future.result() times out, so the real async dispatch (LLM call + its cost-attribution/audit-ledger write) keeps running detached after the step is already reported failed.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: A production INFERENCE_STEP dispatch is bound through SyncDispatcherFacade (wired at harness-runtime/src/harness_runtime/bootstrap/stage_5_loop_init.py around line 549-630). `dispatch()` calls `coro = self.inner.dispatch(...)`, schedules it via `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, self.loop)`, then blocks the CP driver's worker thread on `future.result(timeout=self.result_timeout_seconds)`. If the operator subsequently retries the same workflow run after the FAILED result, a second real dispatch can run concurrently with the still-in-flight orphaned one, i.e. two live LLM calls / two audit writes for logically the same step.

verdict.rationale:
Confirmed as a real defect by direct code read.

1. `sync_dispatcher_facade.py:204-211` — `dispatch()` schedules `coro = self.inner.dispatch(...)` via `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, self.loop)`, then calls `future.result(timeout=self.result_timeout_seconds)`. On the `except TimeoutError` branch it only converts to `StepDispatchTimeoutError` and re-raises — there is no `future.cancel()` call anywhere in the file. `concurrent.futures.Future.result(timeout=...)` is documented Python behavior: on timeout it raises without cancelling the underlying work: the coroutine keeps executing on `self.loop` after the worker thread has already unblocked with an exception.

2. The driver-side consumer confirms the caller-visible consequence: `harness-cp/src/harness_cp/workflow_driver.py:4600-4609` catches `StepDispatchTimeoutError` by name and immediately returns `RunResult(status=RunStatus.FAILED, fail_class="...RT-FAIL-STEP-DISPATCH-TIMEOUT...")` — nothing tracks or waits on the orphaned future.

3. The wrapped coroutine does real, billable, ledger-affecting work: `RuntimeLLMDispatcher.dispatch` (`harness-runtime/.../lifecycle/llm_dispatch.py:2942-2980`) calls `attribute_llm_dispatch_cost(...)` to compute/persist per-attempt cost attribution — i.e. exactly the "cost-attribution/audit-ledger write" the finding describes as an orphaned side effect.

4. The module's own test suite corroborates the gap rather than refuting it: `test_lifecycle_sync_dispatcher_facade.py` D8's docstring (lines 456-463) explicitly states as a "documented limit (not tested here)": cancellation does not propagate to the inner coroutine, and `result_timeout_seconds` bounds only how long the *worker thread* blocks, not how long the inner coroutine keeps running — it can complete (and write) well after the caller has already received a FAILED/cancelled result. This is framed as an accepted-but-real risk tied to spec `C-RT-11 §11` ("in-flight step may be in inconsistent state... CP lifecycle is responsible for transactional discipline if it claims it") — and grep of `workflow_driver.py` confirms no such transactional discipline (dedup/orphan-tracking) actually exists at the `StepDispatchTimeoutError` handling site.

So every mechanical step of the failure scenario is empirically verified against the real code: no cancellation on timeout → orphaned coroutine keeps running on the outer loop → it can still perform a real paid LLM call and append a real cost/audit-ledger entry after the run has already been reported FAILED → its own exception (if it eventually raises one) is never retrieved by any caller (an orphaned `concurrent.futures.Future` whose `.result()`/`.exception()` is never called again is a well-known "exception never retrieved" silent-drop). By contrast, `_project_producer_namespace_attrs` (lines 130-158), used by all 6 producer-specific carriers (Webhook/OperatorBurden/Validator/TrustEvaluation/PauseResume/CostRecord), generically iterates `carrier.model_dump()` and projects every field prefixed `audit_cp_` into `audit.cp.*` — and I confirmed via grep that all 6 producer AuditPayload subclasses (mcp_trust_namespace.py, hitl_webhook_namespace.py, hitl_operator_burden_namespace.py, validator_namespace.py, pause_resume_namespace.py, cost_namespace.py) declare an `audit_cp_prior_event_hash: str` field, so this loop always includes it as `audit.cp.prior_event_hash`.

Ran the actual converter code (uv run) for both a CPAuditLedgerEntry input and a TrustEvaluationAuditPayload input: the CP path's resulting `audit_namespace_attrs` keys are exactly `{action_id, gate_level, response, timestamp}` — no `audit.cp.prior_event_hash` — while the producer path's attrs include `audit.cp.prior_event_hash` alongside action_id/response/timestamp. This directly reproduces the finding's claimed asymmetry.

Also verified the mcp_trust_namespace.py docstring (lines 142-146) explicitly states "the 4 `audit_cp_*` fields are the common CP-sourced field-set... At serialization the payload composes into `AuditPayload.audit_namespace_attrs` as `audit.cp.*`" — confirming the finding's citation and framing that the 4-field contract (action_id, response, timestamp, prior_event_hash) is documented as uniform, but `_project_namespace_attrs` only implements 3 of the 4 for the CPAuditLedgerEntry path. Nothing in the file documents this omission as intentional — the docstring at line 108-114 gives no rationale for excluding prior_event_hash from the namespace-attrs projection.

The only softening point: I found no current downstream consumer in the repo that actually indexes `audit_namespace_attrs['audit.cp.prior_event_hash']` today (grepped harness-od/cxa/cp src for that exact key access — no hits), so the "KeyError" failure_scenario is not something that reproduces against an existing call site right now; it's a latent/schema-shape defect rather than an already-triggered runtime crash. But the core correctness claim — the omission itself, and the cross-path inconsistency relative to the documented 4-common-field contract — is empirically confirmed as real, not a misreading.

srcVerified.summary: verify_chain never validates that a persisted entry's own response_hash matches a fresh recompute of that entry's content, so a corrupted/tampered response_hash field on any non-terminal entry goes undetected.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: Ledger has valid entries E1..E5. Something (disk bit-flip, bad edit, malicious tamper) overwrites E3.response_hash with an arbitrary 32-byte value while leaving E3's other fields and E4.prior_event_hash untouched. verify_chain([E1..E5]) still returns VerificationStatus.VALID with entries_verified=5, because the loop only compares entry[i].prior_event_hash against a freshly recomputed compute_response_hash(entry[i-1]) derived from entry[i-1]'s other fields — it never reads or checks entry[i-1].response_hash itself. Any downstream consumer that trusts a ledger entry's response_hash field as authenticated (e.g. cross-referencing it elsewhere, exporting it to the audit ledger per D5) gets a corrupted value while the chain is reported fully valid. Contrast with the sibling verify_memory_operation_entries() in memory_operation_ledger.py, which explicitly checks `entry.response_hash != compute_memory_operation_response_hash(entry)` and raises RESPONSE_HASH_MISMATCH — the pattern chain_verification.py is missing.

verdict.rationale:
Confirmed as a real defect by direct code read. `harness-is/src/harness_is/chain_verification.py:77-78` loop only checks `ledger[i].prior_event_hash != compute_response_hash(ledger[i - 1])`. Critically, `compute_response_hash` (in `entry_hash.py:105-108`) calls `canonicalize(entry)`, and `canonicalize`'s payload dict (`entry_hash.py:77-99`) deliberately EXCLUDES `entry.response_hash` from the fields it hashes (the docstring even explains why: "response_hash is excluded because it is the field being computed" — avoiding circularity). This means `compute_response_hash(entry[i-1])` never reads or depends on `entry[i-1].response_hash` at all — it is recomputed purely from the other five/seven fields.

Traced the exact failure scenario against the code: for ledger [E1..E5] with only E3.response_hash corrupted (E3's other fields and E4.prior_event_hash untouched), the loop iteration checking E4 computes `compute_response_hash(E3)` from E3's untouched non-response_hash fields — which equals the original correct hash, matching E4.prior_event_hash (also untouched). Every iteration in the loop passes, `verify_chain` returns `VerificationStatus.VALID` with `entries_verified=5`, exactly as the finding describes. Grepped `chain_verification.py` for any access to `.response_hash` — there is none; the field is never read by this module. Also checked `state_ledger_read.py` — zero references to `response_hash`/`compute_response_hash`, so no self-consistency check exists anywhere in the read/verify path.

Confirmed the sibling contrast is accurate: `harness-is/src/harness_is/memory_operation_ledger.py:546` (`verify_memory_operation_entries`) explicitly does `if entry.response_hash != compute_memory_operation_response_hash(entry): ... RESPONSE_HASH_MISMATCH` — the exact self-consistency check that `chain_verification.py` lacks, proving the pattern is known and implementable in this codebase but simply missing from the state-ledger verifier.

Also confirmed downstream consumption is non-trivial: `response_hash` is read/used across `harness-cp` (`workflow_driver.py`, `sub_agent_brief.py`, `pause_resume_protocol.py`, etc.) and `harness-runtime` (`cp_is_wiring.py`, `handoff.py`, `sub_agent_dispatch.py`, `inspect.py`), so a corrupted-but-chain-valid `response_hash` field is not merely inert — it can propagate to consumers that trust the field as authenticated, matching the finding's stated impact.

The one caveat is that `chain_verification.py`'s algorithm is a byte-exact implementation of the canonical spec signature at `Spec_Information_Substrate_v1.md` §6.4 steps 1-4 (which also only checks chain links, not per-entry response_hash self-consistency), so this may also warrant a spec-side note/back-flow — but that does not refute the code-level finding: the described failure scenario is real, reproducible, and exploitable via a corrupted persisted `response_hash` field going completely undetected by `verify_chain`, with entries_verified count and VALID status exactly as claimed.

srcVerified.summary: rollback_to_checkpoint reads and rewrites the JSONL ledger file directly (read_bytes / write_bytes around the git checkout) without acquiring the module-level _WRITE_LOCK that append_ledger_entry/read_ledger use, creating a race that can silently drop a concurrently-appended ledger entry.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: Ledger currently has entries [E1, E2]. Thread/process A calls append_ledger_entry to append E3 (acquires state_ledger_write._WRITE_LOCK, reads ledger, computes E3, opens file in append mode). Concurrently, Thread/process B calls rollback_to_checkpoint on the same ledger_handle: it reads ledger_bytes = ledger_path.read_bytes() (captures [E1, E2] before A's append lands), runs `git checkout <shadow_ref> -- .` (a subprocess call that takes non-trivial wall-clock time), then writes back the stale captured `ledger_bytes` via ledger_path.write_bytes(...) — a full file replace, not an append, and not protected by _WRITE_LOCK. If A's append completes inside that window, B's write_bytes silently overwrites the file back to [E1, E2], permanently losing E3 with no error surfaced to either caller.

verdict.rationale: Confirmed by direct read of both files. state_ledger_write.py defines module-level `_WRITE_LOCK = threading.Lock()` (line 62) and append_ledger_entry() acquires it (line 216 `with _WRITE_LOCK:`) around the entire read-ledger→compute-hash→append-line critical section (lines 217-246), including the actual `fh.write(...)` at line 246. shadow_git_rollback.py never imports or references `_WRITE_LOCK` — its only import from state_ledger_write is `EntryPayload, WriteKey, append_ledger_entry` (line 41). At lines 97-102, rollback_to_checkpoint reads `ledger_bytes = ledger_path.read_bytes()`, then runs `_git(repository_root, 'checkout', shadow_ref, '--', '.')` (a subprocess call, non-trivial wall-clock time), then unconditionally does `ledger_path.write_bytes(ledger_bytes)` — a full-file replace, not an append — with zero locking. This exactly matches the failure scenario: if a concurrent append_ledger_entry call (holding _WRITE_LOCK, invisible to the rollback path) completes its file write during the window between rollback's read_bytes and write_bytes, the rollback's stale write_bytes call silently clobbers the newly-appended entry with no error surfaced to either caller. I also checked test_shadow_git_rollback.py — all 7 tests are single-threaded/sequential; none exercise concurrent append+rollback, so nothing in the test suite catches or contradicts this. The bug is real and matches the finding's mechanism and failure scenario precisely.

srcVerified.summary: emit_secret_fetch_audit hardcodes prior_entry=None on every call and discards the composed StateLedgerEntry, so the hash-chain link is never correct and the entry is never returned/persisted.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: Two secret-fetch events occur in sequence on the same thread (e.g. fetch #1 for an API key, fetch #2 for a DB credential a moment later). emit_secret_fetch_audit is called for both. Each call does `compose_secret_fetch_audit_entry(event_metadata, None)` — per that function's own contract, passing `prior_entry=None` means 'chain inception', producing the ALL_ZEROS_SENTINEL prior_event_hash. So fetch #2's entry is composed as if it were the very first entry in the ledger, even though its true predecessor is fetch #1's entry. Additionally, the returned StateLedgerEntry from compose_secret_fetch_audit_entry is discarded — emit_secret_fetch_audit returns only EmissionResult(emitted=True, rejected_attributes=()), with no field carrying the entry. Any caller trusting emitted=True to mean 'an audit entry with a correct hash-chain link now exists' is wrong: nothing durable or correctly-chained is produced by this call. If this composed-then-discarded entry (or an equivalent one built the same way) is later appended to the shared state ledger, verify_chain would either flag every non-first secret-fetch entry as a broken/tampered link, or — if not strictly enforced — silently defeat the C-IS-06 tamper-evidence guarantee that hash-chaining exists to provide.

verdict.rationale:
The literal code observation is accurate (compose_secret_fetch_audit_entry(event_metadata, None) is called and its return value is discarded; EmissionResult carries no entry field), but the finding's severity/failure-scenario framing does not survive verification against the real code and architecture:

1. Both the module-level and function-level docstrings in secret_fetch_emission.py explicitly document that hash-chain-prior resolution and the durable ledger append are 'runtime concerns' deferred outside this function — this compose-then-discard shape is the documented U-AS-27 contract, not an accidental bug. EmissionResult (shared U-AS-17 schema) never carries an entry payload for any emission function in this file, by design.

2. emit_secret_fetch_audit has zero production callers — confirmed both by a repo-wide grep (only test/definition references) and by the workspace's own prior investigation at .harness/class_1_fork_cxa_1_secret_fetch_audit_bootstrap_ordering.md, which states verbatim that this function 'composes-and-discards' and 'nothing threads a real secret fetch into this machinery — it is speculative substrate.' The operator explicitly ratified a DON'T-WIRE decision for this path (recorded in .harness/roadmap_drift_log_archive.md).

3. Even the actual wired production path (RuntimeAsIsWiring.emit_secret_fetch_audit_entry in harness-runtime/src/harness_runtime/lifecycle/as_is_wiring.py — a completely different function) discards the AS-composed prior_event_hash/response_hash entirely and lets the IS ledger-write contract recompute the chain link internally, per its own docstring. So even where a real append happens, the None-prior composed in secret_fetch_emission.py never reaches the durable ledger.

The failure scenario (two sequential fetches corrupting the shared state ledger's hash chain, caught or missed by verify_chain) requires this discarded entry to actually be appended somewhere — which does not happen anywhere in the current codebase. The scenario is hypothetical/contingent on code that doesn't exist and is contradicted by the documented, already-analyzed architecture.

srcVerified.summary: sandbox_tier_floor() silently falls through to the plain blast-radius floor (no REFUSE, no escalation) when mcp_server is None but mcp_transport indicates a remote/untrusted transport, ignoring the trust semantics encoded in the MCPTransport enum itself.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: Call sandbox_tier_floor(tool, deployment_surface, BlastRadiusTier.READ_ONLY, MCPTransport.STREAMABLE_HTTP_L0_REFUSE, mcp_server=None) — representing a remote MCP server whose transport is explicitly tagged 'L0 refuse' (e.g. because the caller/runtime hasn't yet resolved the MCPServer object, or a bug upstream defaults it to None). Because `tool.forces_computer_use`/`forces_code_execution` are False, `mcp_transport is MCPTransport.STDIO` is False, and `mcp_server is not None` is False, execution falls straight through to `return _resolved(floor)` at rows 7-10, resolving TIER_1_PROCESS — the weakest isolation tier — for a transport that was explicitly named as the refuse-remote case. The MCPTransport enum's own L0/L1/L2/L3 suffix is never consulted anywhere in this function; only `mcp_server.trust_level` is read, and when that object is absent the intended refusal/escalation is silently skipped instead of failing closed (which contradicts the codebase's own stated fail-closed default posture, e.g. RECOMMENDED_CONTRACT_DEFAULT_TIER = TIER_4_FULL_VM).

verdict.rationale:
The finding is refuted. Mechanically, sandbox_tier_floor() at harness-as/src/harness_as/sandbox_tier_floor.py lines 141-155 does skip rows 4-6 (the REFUSE/escalation logic) when mcp_server is None, regardless of mcp_transport's value, falling through to the plain blast-radius floor at line 155 — the finding's mechanical description of the code is accurate in isolation.

However this is confirmed byte-exact, intentional, spec-documented design, not a security defect: design-substrate/Spec_Action_Surface_v1.md §2.3 "Row→argument keying" (line 480) states explicitly that rows 4-6 are keyed SOLELY on mcp_server because "trust level is not derivable from mcp_transport (a Streamable-HTTP server may be any of Level 1/2/3 per §10.3)". The spec deliberately designates mcp_server as sole authority and explicitly disclaims deriving trust from the MCPTransport enum's L0/L1/L2/L3 suffix — directly contradicting the finding's framing that the function "ignores the trust semantics encoded in the MCPTransport enum itself" as if that were an omission.

Additionally, the failure scenario does not reproduce at any real call site: every production caller (harness-runtime/src/harness_runtime/config/sandbox_defaults.py:243-253, harness-as/src/harness_as/gate_level_composition.py, harness-as/src/harness_as/sandbox_tier_composition.py) constructs mcp_transport and mcp_server together from the same MCPClientConfig registration entry (entry.transport + MCPServer(trust_level=entry.trust_level)), so the mismatched combination (transport set, server None) the finding requires never occurs in practice. sandbox_defaults.py even documents that the REFUSE path is normally unreachable at that site because L0-remote servers are refused at registration before reaching this resolver. A separate, required-argument function (mcp_transport_floor() in mcp_transport_floor.py) is the actual production gate for per-transport trust and has no such Optional-argument gap. The finding constructs a synthetic call pattern that violates the documented contract rather than exposing a reachable production defect.

srcVerified.summary: verify_hash_chain_integrity never recomputes an entry's own entry_hash from its payload, so it cannot detect a tampered/corrupted audit-ledger entry — it only checks that consecutive stored hash fields link up.
srcVerified.failure_scenario: An AuditLedger entry's payload (e.g. audit_namespace_attrs holding a cost or HITL-response value) is mutated in place (by a bug, a bad migration, or a compromised writer) while the stored entry_hash field is left unchanged, and the following entry's prior_entry_hash is also left unchanged (it still equals the unchanged entry_hash). Calling verify_hash_chain_integrity(ledger) walks the chain checking only entries[i].payload.prior_entry_hash == entries[i-1].entry_hash for i>0; since neither stored hash field was touched, this check passes and the function returns None (well-formed) even though the payload no longer matches the SHA-256 that entry_hash is supposed to certify. Contrast: the sibling function verify_rotation_pairs in the same file does call compute_entry_hash(entry.payload) and compares it against entry.entry_hash before trusting an entry — the general-purpose verifier omits exactly that check, defeating the audit ledger's core tamper-evidence purpose.

verdict.rationale:
CONFIRMED by direct code read + empirical execution. Read harness-od/src/harness_od/multi_tenant_trace_separation_and_audit_ledger.py:238-257 (verify_hash_chain_integrity) and its sibling verify_rotation_pairs:340-422. verify_hash_chain_integrity's loop body is exactly: `prior_hash = entries[i].payload.prior_entry_hash; predecessor_hash = entries[i-1].entry_hash; if prior_hash != predecessor_hash: raise HashChainBreach`. It never calls compute_entry_hash(entry.payload) to recompute and compare against the entry's own stored entry_hash. This is confirmed as the documented, intentional scope by AuditLedger's own docstring in audit_ledger_types.py:126-129 ('Well-formedness invariant: entries[i].payload.prior_entry_hash == entries[i-1].entry_hash ... verification is U-OD-30's verify_hash_chain_integrity'), and further corroborated by verify_rotation_pairs's own docstring/comment (lines 353-358) which explicitly notes it (unlike the general walk) recomputes entry_hash via compute_entry_hash before trusting an entry, catching 'a payload mutated in place ... with a stale entry_hash left behind.' The module docstring (lines 32-41) further states the OD-local walk 'composes with the IS C-IS-10 §10.3 hash-chain integrity primitive at 7c' — i.e., recompute-based tamper detection is deferred to a cross-axis composition that is NOT yet wired in this file, meaning as shipped today the gap is live, not merely theoretical.

I then empirically reproduced the exact failure scenario by running real code against the actual types (harness-od venv, uv run): built a 2-entry AuditLedger where entry 0's payload audit_namespace_attrs (a cost.usd value) was mutated from '1.00' to '999999.00' via model_copy while its stored entry_hash field was left at the original (now-stale) value, and entry 1's prior_entry_hash still pointed at that same unchanged stale hash. Output: `compute_entry_hash(tampered_payload) != tampered_e0.entry_hash` is True (the stored hash no longer matches the payload), yet `verify_hash_chain_integrity(tampered_ledger)` returned `None` with no exception — the tamper was silently accepted. This exactly matches the finding's failure_scenario. The finding's category/severity framing (high/security) is reasonable for a deployment-preflight review of an audit-ledger tamper-evidence primitive, and the contrast drawn against verify_rotation_pairs (which does call compute_entry_hash and compare) is accurate — I read that function's body directly (lines 382-390) and it does exactly that.

srcUnverified.summary: verify_rotation_6_steps hardcodes succeeded=True for every step of the key-rotation verification protocol regardless of scope or actual state, so execute_key_rotation always reports rotation_complete=True.
srcUnverified.failure_scenario: The function signature takes `scope: SigningKeyScope` but immediately discards it (`_ = scope`) and returns a StepResult(succeeded=True, ...) for all 6 steps unconditionally — there is no actual dual-key verification, hash-chain continuity check, or secret-fetch validation performed. execute_key_rotation() then computes `complete = all(s.succeeded for s in steps)`, which is always True, and reports final_stage=ROW_2_RETIRE_OLD (old key retired) even if, e.g., the new key was never actually staged or the hash-chain link across the rotation boundary is genuinely broken. The two-row key-rotation safety protocol is effectively a no-op that always signals success.

srcUnverified.summary: compute_child_blast_radius_ceiling always returns BlastRadiusTier.READ_ONLY regardless of the parent's tier, contradicting its own docstring's claim that Tier-1/Tier-2 parents 'pass the floor through unchanged', and contradicting the module-level C-CP-12 §12.1 disposition table that says local-mutation is INHERIT (not downgraded).
srcUnverified.failure_scenario: A LOCAL_MUTATION-tier (Tier-2) parent dispatching a sub-agent expects (per the module docstring's own per-tool-class table: 'local-mutation INHERIT') the sub-agent to retain LOCAL_MUTATION-tier tool access. Instead compute_child_blast_radius_ceiling(BlastRadiusTier.LOCAL_MUTATION) returns READ_ONLY (line 77: `_ = parent; return BlastRadiusTier.READ_ONLY` unconditionally), so any caller relying on this function's own docstring ('Tier-1/Tier-2 parents pass the floor through unchanged') to compute the child ceiling will incorrectly deny legitimate local-mutation tool calls to sub-agents dispatched from Tier-2 parents, breaking otherwise-permitted workflows (fail-closed, but a functional correctness defect against the documented contract).

srcUnverified.summary: CollectorDaemonSupervisor.stop() catches asyncio.CancelledError from its own await without re-raising, silently swallowing cancellation of the stop() coroutine itself.
srcUnverified.failure_scenario: A caller bounds the shutdown sequence with `await asyncio.wait_for(supervisor.stop(), timeout=X)` (or otherwise cancels the task running stop()). If the cancellation lands while stop() is inside `await asyncio.wait_for(self._task, timeout=timeout_seconds)`, that inner wait_for propagates asyncio.CancelledError, which `stop()`'s `except (TimeoutError, asyncio.CancelledError):` clause catches and does not re-raise — it just calls `self._task.cancel()` and continues to set `self._health = STOPPED` and return normally. The outer canceller never observes the CancelledError, so the bounded-shutdown wrapper cannot actually enforce its timeout on this call, and (per normal asyncio semantics) suppressing a task's own cancellation this way is the anti-pattern of swallowing the current coroutine's cancellation instead of re-raising it.

srcUnverified.summary: attribute_tool_dispatch_cost() (and its validator-dispatch sibling) accepts a caller-composed `idempotency_key` parameter that is never used anywhere in the function body -- the SpanCostRecord's idempotency_key is instead unconditionally set to `parent_idempotency_key` via `cost_chain.attach_idempotency_key`.
srcUnverified.failure_scenario: runtime_tool_dispatcher.py composes a dispatch-specific idempotency_key via `_compose_idempotency_key` (documented at cost_attribution_tool_dispatch.py:220-223 as 'Tool-dispatch idempotency key composed at runtime_tool_dispatcher.py:401') and passes it into `attribute_tool_dispatch_cost(idempotency_key=idempotency_key, ...)`; the identical pattern recurs in cost_attribution_validator_dispatch.py (`attribute_validator_dispatch_cost`, line ~119, where the caller composes `f"validator:{workflow_id}:{step.step_id}"`). In both functions the `idempotency_key` argument is read nowhere in the body -- `SpanCostRecord(idempotency_key="", ...)` is built and then immediately overwritten by `cost_chain.attach_idempotency_key(span_id, parent_idempotency_key, cost_record)`, whose OD implementation (harness-od/src/harness_od/idempotency_join_dedup.py `attach_idempotency_key_to_cost_record`) sets `idempotency_key` to `parent_idempotency_key`, not to the passed-in per-dispatch key. The sibling LLM-dispatch precedent (`cost_attribution_llm_dispatch.py:attribute_llm_dispatch_cost`) has no such parameter at all, confirming the design intent is `parent_idempotency_key`-only. Any maintainer reading the docstring ('Tool-dispatch idempotency key composed at ... step 6') would reasonably believe this key distinguishes per-dispatch cost records; it is silently discarded, so the elaborate per-call key composition at the caller site is dead work and any future code that assumes it is actually threaded through (e.g. for per-dispatch replay/dedup keying) would be operating on a false premise.

srcUnverified.summary: _content_from_record() swallows every exception from base64-decoding a stored memory record's content and returns None, which downstream callers treat identically to 'no content was ever written' rather than 'stored content is corrupted'.
srcUnverified.failure_scenario: If a `content_b64` field in a persisted MemoryStoreRecord is ever malformed (e.g. truncated write, storage-layer bit-flip, or a future producer bug that stores non-base64 text), `_content_from_record` catches the broad `Exception` from `base64.b64decode(..., validate=True)` and returns `None`. `view()` at line 116-117 then raises `MemoryCallbackIOError(f"view({path!r}) failed: not found")` -- the same error an operator sees for a path that was genuinely never written -- so real data corruption is silently reported as ordinary absence, hiding an integrity problem an operator would otherwise want surfaced distinctly (e.g. to trigger a re-migration or an alert) instead of being told the memory simply doesn't exist.

srcUnverified.summary: Full-jitter retry backoff is computed twice with independent random draws — the OTel span records one delay value while a different (unrelated) delay value is what is actually slept.
srcUnverified.failure_scenario: In `_run_per_candidate_attempts`, on a transient failure that will be retried (STAGE_2_RETRY_WITH_BACKOFF, not last attempt), line 877 calls `backoff_seconds = self.retry_breaker.compute_delay_seconds(attempt)` and records `retry.delay_ms = int(backoff_seconds * 1000)` on the `harness.runtime.retry_attempt` span. After the span context manager exits, line 941 calls `await self.sleep_fn(self.retry_breaker.compute_delay_seconds(attempt))` — a SECOND, independent call to the same function with the same `attempt` index. `compute_full_jitter_delay_seconds` draws from `random.uniform(0, bounded)` with no shared/seeded `rng` in production (`RuntimeRetryBreaker.compute_delay_seconds` defaults `rng=None`), so the two calls produce statistically independent random values from the same range. Concretely, for `attempt=2`, base=0.5s, cap=30s: call #1 might draw 3.1s (recorded as `retry.delay_ms=3100` on the span) while call #2 (the actual `asyncio.sleep` duration) draws 0.4s — the harness sleeps 0.4s but its own telemetry claims it waited 3.1s. This directly contradicts the adjacent code comment ("We sleep after recording the attempt terminal so the inner span carries the actually-elapsed backoff hint") — the span does NOT carry the actually-elapsed backoff; it carries an unrelated random sample. Any operator/dashboard/cost-latency-analysis trusting `retry.delay_ms` for this span is misled on every transient retry.

srcUnverified.summary: The per-path asyncio.Lock is keyed by the raw callback path string, not the canonicalized resolved filesystem path, so two textually-different paths that resolve to the same file bypass the documented single-authoritative-lock atomicity guarantee.
srcUnverified.failure_scenario: `_validate_path` only rejects `..` traversal segments and a literal `//` immediately after the `/memories/` prefix; it does not reject other redundant forms. `PurePosixPath('a//b.md').parts == ('a','b.md')` and `PurePosixPath('a/./b.md').parts == ('a','b.md')` (verified empirically), so paths like `/memories/notes/a//file.md` and `/memories/notes/a/file.md` (or forms with a `./` segment) both pass validation and resolve via `.resolve()` to the identical filesystem path, yet `self._locks[path]` keys on the original un-normalized string, producing two DIFFERENT asyncio.Lock objects for the same file. Two concurrent tool calls using these two string forms of the same path (e.g. from parallel tool_use blocks in one agent turn) can both enter str_replace/insert unserialized: both read the same original content, both compute an edit from that stale content, and the second write silently clobbers the first's edit — a lost-update race that contradicts the module's own documented invariant ('the codec runs INSIDE the existing per-path lock so the single source of truth for read-modify-write atomicity... stays this backend's per-path lock').

srcUnverified.summary: compute_delay_seconds(attempt) is called twice per retry — once to populate the retry.delay_ms span attribute, once for the actual sleep — and since it samples from random.uniform (full-jitter, non-deterministic), the two calls return different values, so the recorded telemetry does not match the real delay applied.

srcUnverified.summary: Concurrent-writer serialization for the JSONL state ledger relies on a module-level threading.Lock, which only mutually excludes writers within one Python process; the docstring's acceptance #7 claim does not hold for concurrent OS processes appending to the same ledger file (e.g. separate sub-agent/CLI-profile processes sharing a worktree's state ledger).

Each process has its own independent _WRITE_LOCK object, so neither blocks the other. Both read the same last entry E_N, both compute prior_event_hash = compute_response_hash(E_N) for their respective new entries, and both append a line with an identical prior_event_hash — corrupting the chain (chain_verification.verify_chain will later report a CHAIN_LINK_MISMATCH for whichever entry lands second, and the two entries are not distinguishable as duplicates because they generally carry different idempotency_key values, so the idempotent-noop path does not save them).

testFindings.summary: test_signed_with_ed25519_default asserts a tautology instead of checking the entry's actual signature algorithm

testFindings.summary: No test ever constructs a MemoryOperationEntry/MemoryOperationPayload with a mismatched operation_kind/operation_projection pair or an inconsistent redaction_event, so MemoryOperationProjectionMismatchError and MemoryOperationRedactionEventMismatchError (memory_operation_ledger.py lines 147, 182, 195, 199, 206, 210) are entirely unexercised anywhere in the suite.

testFindings.summary: The retrieval test file (3 tests, all happy-path) never exercises the MemoryRetrievalResult._hashes_match_packet model_validator (packet_hash/selected_refs cross-consistency, memory_retrieval.py lines 159-163) nor the retrieval canonicalization TypeErrors; it also never calls MemoryRetriever.retrieve() before the derived retrieval index has been rebuilt.

(b) MemoryRetriever.retrieve() calls index_store.read_current() with no exception handling; on a cold-start retrieval (no rebuild() has ever run) this raises an uncaught DerivedRetrievalIndexMissingError instead of returning an empty/graceful result — a realistic first-run production scenario with zero test coverage.

testFindings.summary: The model_validator branch at cli_profile.py:186 ("CLI provider identity binding requires provider, kind, and command" — partial provider-binding fields) is never exercised; only the fully-generic and fully-specified branches are tested via the 4 existing pytest.raises calls.

If a future change to _WORKLOAD_CLASS_FAVORED, ENGINE_CLASS_CANDIDATES, or _persona_tier_admits accidentally makes the message-formatting, exception type, or the raise condition itself wrong (e.g. swallowed exception, wrong exception class, or the guard silently returning a default engine class instead of aborting), no test would go red — the docstring's own admission ('the error path is exercised via the unreachable-surface guard') shows the author knew this branch was never actually hit.

testFindings.summary: MultiTenantOverrideRefusedError (raised by RedactionSpanProcessor.__init__ when persona_tier=MULTI_TENANT_COMPLIANCE and redacted_attributes is empty) is never imported or exercised anywhere in this file, and a repo-wide grep confirms it is not referenced in any test file in this directory.

testFindings.summary: test_committed_surface_frozen_and_hashable asserts `hash(surface) == hash(surface)` (an object hashed against itself), which is tautologically true for any object regardless of whether __hash__ is field-based or falls back to identity-based hashing; the test then builds a `duplicate` record and checks `surface == duplicate` but never checks `hash(surface) == hash(duplicate)`, so the load-bearing dataclass invariant (equal objects must hash equal, required for correct dict/set membership) is never actually verified. The sibling test at line 117 (test_deferred_surface_frozen_and_hashable) has the same pattern.
testFindings.failure_scenario: If the frozen record's __hash__ were accidentally derived from something other than its field values (e.g. object identity, or a subset of fields excluding one that participates in __eq__), this test would still pass, while at runtime two logically-equal CommittedSurface/DeferredSurface instances could land in different buckets of a dict/set, silently duplicating or dropping entries wherever these records are used as keys/set members.

testFindings.summary: test_transition_record_frozen_and_hashable asserts `hash(transition) == hash(transition)`, comparing the same object instance to itself instead of two distinct-but-equal instances (the correct pattern is used elsewhere in this same test suite, e.g. test_observability_matrix.py and test_rate_table_types.py, which construct `a` and `b` separately and assert `hash(a) == hash(b)`).
testFindings.failure_scenario: A regression that breaks field-based __hash__ consistency for BridgingArcTransition (e.g. hash falling back to id()-based default, or a field being excluded from __hash__ but not __eq__) would go undetected, risking silent dict/set-membership bugs anywhere BridgingArcTransition records are deduplicated or used as keys.

testFindings.summary: test_cell_dashboard_binding_frozen_and_hashable asserts `hash(binding) == hash(binding)` on a single object instance rather than comparing two separately-constructed but field-equal CellDashboardBinding instances, so it does not verify the equal-objects-hash-equal invariant.
testFindings.failure_scenario: A hash-implementation regression on CellDashboardBinding (e.g. drifting from field-based hashing) would not be caught, risking silent duplicate/lost entries if this record is ever used as a dict key or set member in dashboard-binding lookups.

testFindings.summary: test_posture_model_frozen_and_hashable asserts `hash(posture) == hash(posture)` (self-comparison) before constructing a `duplicate` record for an equality check a few lines later, but never asserts hash equality between the original and the duplicate.
testFindings.failure_scenario: Same class of gap as the other frozen/hashable tests in this suite: a broken field-based __hash__ on PerPersonaTierRedactionPosture would not be caught by this test, risking silent dict/set-membership inconsistency for redaction-posture records.

testFindings.summary: test_dispatcher_without_cost_substrate_silently_skips_cost_attribution asserts nothing about the claimed 'silently skips' behavior — it only calls dispatch() and relies on 'no exception raised'
testFindings.failure_scenario: If a future regression causes the dispatcher, when constructed without cost_chain/audit_writer/rate_table, to still attempt a partial or malformed cost-attribution write (e.g. via an incorrect default fallback that doesn't crash, or a duck-typed no-op object that silently accepts calls but corrupts shared state), this test would stay green because it never inspects the audit ledger or the OTel span attributes for absence of a COST_ATTRIBUTED_DECIMAL_ATTR / audit entry — unlike the sibling positive test just above it (lines ~296-315) which does assert `len(audit_writer.appended) == 1` and the cost span attribute. The negative counterpart never performs the mirrored absence-checks.

testFindings.summary: test_antigravity_cli_auth_confirms_antigravity_route and test_gemini_legacy_cli_auth_confirms_gemini_legacy_route (line 148) always call pytest.skip() unconditionally after the PATH check — there is no code path under which either test can ever execute or pass
testFindings.failure_scenario: These two test functions are permanently inert regardless of environment (CLI installed+authenticated or not); if an Antigravity/Gemini auth-route regression were introduced in `resolve_cli_profile` or `ExternalCliRoute` construction for those two providers specifically, neither test could ever catch it because the body unconditionally skips before reaching the route-resolution assertions that the sibling Claude Code/Codex tests exercise (lines 93-139). They read as coverage for 4 CLI providers but only 2 are ever actually exercised.

testFindings.summary: No test exercises any of the helper module's validation/error branches (invalid --provider choice, generic-command missing --provider-name/--command/--model/--family).
testFindings.failure_scenario: tools/external_cli_provider_config.py has 5 `raise ValueError(...)` branches guarding required fields for the generic-command provider path (lines ~160-233). All 4 tests in this file only exercise happy paths (codex, generic-command with all fields supplied, gemini CLI, antigravity CLI). If a refactor accidentally makes `--model` or `--family` optional for generic-command (e.g. defaults to None and gets silently written into the materialized TOML), the test suite stays green while a malformed/incomplete external-CLI routing config could be materialized and consumed downstream by `just <provider>-live-e2e` recipes.

testFindings.summary: materialize_r_cxa_2_producer_loop_stage's four precondition-guard error branches (missing cp_is_wiring, hitl_registry, ask_user_question_surface, tool_dispatcher) are never exercised by pytest.raises anywhere in this file.
testFindings.failure_scenario: The source (harness_runtime/bootstrap/factories/r_cxa_2_producer_loop_factory.py lines 248-266) raises RCXA2ProducerLoopMaterializeError with a distinct message for each of 4 missing-context-field preconditions before stage-5 LOOP_INIT can bind R-CXA-2 producer loops. If a future edit inverts one of these `is None` checks, deletes a guard, or the guard's condition drifts out of sync with an upstream stage-ordering change (e.g. stage 3b no longer populating ctx.hitl_registry before stage 5 runs), this test suite would stay green while bootstrap either silently proceeds with a null dependency (later NPE deep in RuntimeHITLToolLoop/RuntimeEngineRecoveryLoop construction with a much less actionable traceback) or fails with a wrong/misleading error class. Sibling factories in the same bootstrap/factories/ family (webhook_delivery_composer_factory.py, skill_activation_emitter_factory.py) both have their analogous *MaterializeError guard raises covered by pytest.raises in their own test files, making this file's omission a real outlier rather than an intentional scope choice.

testFindings.summary: The completeness-gate detector `violations()` is only ever called against the live, already-clean matrix — no test constructs a matrix with a known contract-missing-test-evidence or CXA-seam-missing-endpoint row and asserts `violations()` reports it.
testFindings.failure_scenario: If `qa_evidence_matrix.violations()` regressed (e.g. the `if not row["test_files"]:` check got inverted, or the CXA-missing loop got dropped/short-circuited), this test file would stay green because the live repo state happens to have zero violations today — the detector's actual catching behavior is unverified.

testFindings.summary: `assert out.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == report` only proves the filesystem round-trips a string written on the previous line — it adds no coverage of `render_markdown` beyond the substring assertions already made above it.
testFindings.failure_scenario: This assertion cannot fail for any reason related to `render_markdown` correctness; it can only fail on a filesystem/encoding bug in the test's own `write_text`/`read_text` calls, so it masquerades as verification while checking nothing about production code.

testFindings.summary: `_green_delegates` mocks `_run`, `_roadmap_status`, `_arc_snapshot`, and `_overlay_orphans` for all three tests in the file, but every test asserts only the manual-signoff predicates (G1.4/G1.7/G1.8) from `closure_gate.evaluate()`; the five automatable Tier-1 predicates (G1.1 forward-register-empty, G1.2 arc-ledger --check exit code, G1.3 contract orphans, G1.5 CXA seam orphans, G1.6 substitution-ledger --check exit code) and all six Tier-2 predicates (G2.1–G2.6 roadmap RESOLVED checks) are never asserted on in this file.
testFindings.failure_scenario: An inverted or broken condition in `evaluate()` for any of G1.1/G1.2/G1.3/G1.5/G1.6/G2.1-G2.6 (e.g. `rc == 0` becoming `rc != 0` for the `arc_ledger.py --check` or `substitution_ledger.py --check` delegated exit-code checks, or the roadmap-status RESOLVED comparison being flipped) would not turn any test in this file red, even though those are exactly the automatable predicates the closure gate exists to enforce.
